title: Multiplication using factors and known facts

beats.say: Open like a teacher: you don't need to learn every fact separately; one fact you know can unlock many you don't. Playful tone. No questions.

lines.say: Here's something nobody tells you: you don't have to memorise every multiplication fact. Say you know six times seven is forty-two. Then six times fourteen, which you may not know, is almost free. Let me show you.

beats.say: Doubling: 14 is double 7, so 6 x 14 is double 6 x 7 = 84. Explain in words: if one factor is doubled and the other stays the same, the product doubles. No questions.

lines.say: We know six sevens are forty-two. We want six fourteens.
Look at fourteen: it's double seven. It's two sevens.
So six fourteens is two lots of six sevens. Two forty-twos. Double forty-two is eighty-four.

lines.text: Double one factor  →  the product doubles
lines.say: The rule: double one of the numbers, keep the other the same, and the answer doubles.

beats.say: Halving and swapping: from 6 x 8 = 48 find 3 x 8: 3 is half of 6, so half of 48 = 24. Also order doesn't matter: 8 x 6 = 6 x 8. No questions.

lines.say: The same idea works the other way round. We know six eights are forty-eight. What about three eights?

lines.text: 3 is half of 6, so half of 48
lines.say: Three is half of six, so three eights is half of forty-eight.
Half of forty-eight is twenty-four.
And one more trick: you can swap the order. Eight sixes are the same as six eights. So every fact you learn gives you two.

beats.say: A friend thinks 6 x 14 = 42 + 14 = 56 (adds 7 more). Test: 6 x 10 is already 60. Detective tone. No questions.

lines.say: A friend of mine said: fourteen is seven more than seven, so I add fourteen to forty-two. That gives fifty-six. Let's test it.
Here's their sum, fifty-six.
But six tens is already sixty, and six fourteens has even more than six tens. So fifty-six is too small.

lines.text: Doubling a factor DOUBLES the answer. It doesn't add on.
lines.say: Doubling the factor doubles the whole answer. It doesn't just add a bit on.

beats.say: Splitting a factor: 5 x 12 where 12 = 3 x 4. Multiply by 3, then by 4. No questions.

lines.say: Here's another trick. Five times twelve. Twelve can be split into three times four, two smaller factors.
So multiply by the three first: five threes are fifteen.
Then by the four: fifteen fours are sixty. So five twelves are sixty.

beats.say: The toolkit in four lines. No questions.

lines.text: DOUBLE one factor  →  double the answer
lines.say: First tool: double one of the numbers, and the answer doubles as well.

lines.text: HALVE one factor  →  halve the answer
lines.say: Second tool: halve one of the numbers, and the answer halves too.
Third tool: swap which number comes first, and nothing changes.

lines.text: SPLIT a factor into smaller factors, multiply one after the other
lines.say: And fourth: break a factor into smaller ones, and multiply one step at a time.

beats.say: Do one TOGETHER: 4 x 8 = 32, find 4 x 16. Questions written on the board first.

lines.say: Now you help me. We know four eights are thirty-two. We want four sixteens.
Yes, sixteen is double eight.

ask.onMiss: Ask: what do you multiply 8 by to get 16?

lines.say: So the answer doubles too: double thirty-two.

ask.onMiss: Ask: if 16 is double 8, what happens to the answer 32?

beats.say: The child works alone: 5 x 6 = 30 so 5 x 12; 9 x 4 = 36 so 9 x 8; then explain why doubling works. Hints only if stuck.

lines.say: Your turn to lead. Two facts you know, and two you can now work out without learning them.
Twelve is double six, so double thirty.

ask.onMiss: Ask: how is 12 related to 6? So what happens to 30?

lines.say: Eight is double four, so double thirty-six.

lines.text: Twice as many groups gives twice as many in total
lines.say: The reason it works.

ask.prompt: In your own words: why does doubling a factor double the answer?
ask.lookFor: Doubling one factor means twice as many equal groups (or twice as big), so twice the total.
ask.onMiss: Ask: 5 groups of 6, then 5 groups of 12: how much bigger is each group?
